land.text: Cisplatina, the land in Brazil's 1827 shape and not in its 1828 shape

predecessors.note: Cisplatina, the Brazilian province, independent by the Preliminary Peace Convention of 27 August 1828.

land.text: the Eastern Province, which the Florida assembly of 25 August 1825 had declared united with the United Provinces

predecessors.note: Claimed by the United Provinces during the Cisplatine War; held by Brazil in 1825-1828.

capitals.name: Montevideo
capitals.note: 'Capital and largest city: Montevideo' (infobox). Besieged by Oribe's Cerrito government from February 1843 for nine years.

keyframe_review.note: 180,732 km2 for 1828-1864 against the infobox's 'approximately 176,215 square kilometers' (ratio 1.03): the whole of today's Uruguay. The state begins on 27 August 1828 (infobox 'Recognized: 27 August 1828'; the Cisplatine War page has the Preliminary Peace Convention of that date and the Treaty of Montevideo). The shape runs through the Guerra Grande (the Cerrito and Defence governments, 1843-1851) and the 1851 treaties, in which, the Uruguayan Civil War page says, Uruguay 'renounced its territorial claims north of the Río Cuareim'; those claims are outside the shape, so it needs no change.

180,631 km2 for 1865 alone, 102 km2 below the neighbouring shapes: a one-year artifact. The Uruguayan War (10 August 1864 - 20 February 1865) put Brazilian garrisons in Melo, Salto, Paysandu, Fray Bentos and Colonia, but the page reports no change to Uruguay's borders: the outline stands and the occupation is carried by the ledger's contest events.

180,732 km2 for 1866-2023, the same outline as 1828 (ratio 1.03 to the infobox's 176,215 km2). The page names two Brazilian boundary disputes (Isla Brasilera and a 235 km2 Invernada River region near Masoller) that 'remain de facto under Brazilian control'; both are below the resolution of the shape.

region.text: the Eastern Republic of Uruguay, centred on Montevideo

ledger.note: 27 August 1828: Cisplatina becomes the Eastern Republic of Uruguay. Argentine and Brazilian representatives, under British mediation, signed the Preliminary Peace Convention on 27 August 1828 and the Treaty of Montevideo acknowledged Cisplatina's independence 'under the name Eastern Republic of Uruguay'. The infobox gives 'Declared: 25 August 1825' and 'Recognized: 27 August 1828'; the first constitution was adopted on 18 July 1830.

region.text: Cisplatina, the land in Brazil's 1827 shape and not in its 1828 shape

ledger.note: 27 August 1828: the whole of Cisplatina passes from Brazil to the new republic (the Brazil dossier records the matching loss).

region.text: the interior of Uruguay held by Oribe's Cerrito government, all but Montevideo

ledger.note: February 1843: Oribe besieges Montevideo and splits the country. 'The siege of Montevideo began in February 1843 and lasted nine years' (Uruguay page); after Arroyo Grande (6 December 1842) the Gobierno del Cerrito under Manuel Oribe governed the rest of the country (1843-1851) while the Gobierno de la Defensa under Joaquin Suarez governed Montevideo (1843-1852). The Defence government in Montevideo is treated as the Uruguayan state.

region.text: the interior of Uruguay held by Oribe's Cerrito government

ledger.note: 1851: Oribe is defeated and the Colorados hold the whole country. 'Manuel Oribe was defeated in 1851, leaving the Colorados in full control of the country'; 'Brazil followed up by intervening in Uruguay in May 1851'. The page gives no month for the end of the siege.

region.text: the places Brazilian forces took: Melo (Cerro Largo), Salto, Paysandu, Fray Bentos (Rio Negro) and Colonia del Sacramento

ledger.note: 14 October 1864: Brazil invades Uruguay. A Brazilian brigade invaded Uruguay's Cerro Largo Department on 14 October and entered Melo on 16 October; Salto was garrisoned after November 1864, Fray Bentos taken from 1 January 1865, Paysandu overrun on 2 January 1865 and Colonia occupied in January 1865. The year and month are the page's; the union of departments is the researcher's reading of the towns.

region.text: the places Brazilian forces took: Melo (Cerro Largo), Salto, Paysandu, Fray Bentos (Rio Negro) and Colonia del Sacramento

ledger.note: 20 February 1865: the Villa de la Union accord ends the Uruguayan War. Flores and Herrera y Obes 'signed a peace accord on 20 February at the Villa de la Unión' and Flores took the presidency; the page does not say when Brazilian forces withdrew (Fray Bentos later served as a Brazilian base).

wars.name: Cisplatine War

zones.text: Cisplatina, the land in Brazil's 1827 shape and not in its 1828 shape

wars.outcome: The Preliminary Peace Convention of 27 August 1828, mediated by Britain, made Cisplatina independent as the Eastern Republic of Uruguay.
wars.note: The Florida assembly of 25 August 1825 declared independence from Brazil and union with the United Provinces; Brazil declared war on 10 December 1825; Ituzaingo was fought on 20 February 1827.

wars.name: Uruguayan Civil War (Guerra Grande)

zones.text: the interior held by the Cerrito government

wars.outcome: The Cerrito government of Oribe, with Rosas's forces, held the interior and besieged Montevideo from February 1843; Oribe was defeated in 1851 after Urquiza's uprising against Rosas and Brazil's May 1851 intervention, and five treaties with Brazil followed.
wars.note: The page dates the war 1839-1851 officially and the broader conflict to 1832; Oribe resigned on 24 October 1838 and Rivera 'completely crushed' him at Palmar on 15 June 1838. Rivera was defeated at Arroyo Grande on 6 December 1842.

wars.name: Uruguayan War

zones.text: the places Brazilian forces took: Melo (Cerro Largo), Salto, Paysandu, Fray Bentos (Rio Negro) and Colonia del Sacramento

wars.outcome: Brazil and the Colorados won: Flores took the presidency on 20 February 1865 under the Villa de la Union accord; Uruguay's borders did not change.
wars.note: The page gives the war as 10 August 1864 - 20 February 1865; Paraguay's seizure of the Marques de Olinda (12 November 1864) and invasion of Mato Grosso (26 December 1864) followed.

certainty.note: No treaty fixed the Brazilian frontier before 1851; the claim north of the Rio Cuareim was open.
The Brazil-Uruguay boundary is defined 'according to the 1851 border treaty'; the Isla Brasilera and Invernada (Masoller) disputes are small exceptions.

notes:
Four pages opened (the budget is five). The Uruguay article gave identity, the 176,215 km2 area and the 1851 border treaty; the Cisplatine War page the 27 August 1828 convention; the Uruguayan War page the 1864-1865 Brazilian invasion; the Uruguayan Civil War page the two-government period 1843-1851.

Cliopatria's four shapes are the same outline (180,732 km2) throughout, so the shape review is short; the work is in the ledger. Rows to add or reassign: the Gobierno del Cerrito (Oribe's government, 1843-1851, the interior of Uruguay) is a civil-war state Cliopatria lacks; slug gobierno-del-cerrito, type rebel, written by this batch if time allowed (see the report). The Empire of Brazil dossier (another part of am-08) has the matching loss of Cisplatina on 27 August 1828 but no contest for the 1864-1865 Brazilian invasion nor any record of Brazil's client relation after the 1851 treaties (the Uruguay page: the 1851 treaties 'confirmed Brazil's right to intervene in Uruguay's internal affairs' and 'Brazil intervened militarily in Uruguay as often as it deemed necessary'); that relation would be vassal_start events in Brazil's dossier, which no page opened dates an end for.
Not settled: the Argentine side of the Guerra Grande (Rosas's blockade of Montevideo and Oribe's army); the date the Brazilian garrisons of 1864-1865 left; the Rincon de Artigas and Isla Brasilera boundary dates (not on the Uruguay page); the oath of 18 July 1830 (the Cisplatine page does not carry it).
